$comment: A DDS-only walkthrough, modelled field for field on the base game's Nice_Place tree (688dcc47-3b4a-41fd-9b20-c1132c9814dd) so that its gating is copied rather than invented. Six parts: the tree and what makes it fire, who is talking, the four remaining messages, the links that chain them, the replacements that make one line three, and the ending that varies. Steps point at a whole document window and name the key in their text -- highlighting a row did not survive contact with the tree. A tree's file name is the GUID it was given on creation, so no step can name it: the documents are pointed at by window (#file-window-0 the tree, -1 the message, -2 the block) and the lines are checked in the mod's dds.blocks.csv, whose path is fixed. Steps gated on savedText read the file from disk, so they need Autosaving left on.

steps.title: Pick a mod to build in
steps.description:
Choose a mod, and a content folder inside it. Everything this walkthrough makes goes under that folder's DDSContent, and nothing else in the mod is touched.

Leave Autosaving on: the steps ahead check your work by reading the files.

steps.title: Start a conversation
steps.description:
Click Add new....

You are going to build a chat between two citizens about playing Wizcards on their crunchers — the same shape as the small talk the base game already puts in bars and diners.

steps.title: Name it, and give it its first line
steps.description: Choose Tree from the Type dropdown, name it WizcardsChat, and put You still playing Wizcards? in the English line.

steps.title: Three documents, not one
steps.description:
A tree, the message inside it, and the block inside that — one window each, left to right.

The split is the whole point of the format. The tree is the conversation: who is in it, when it happens, and which message follows which. A message is one thing said. A block is the words, and the words themselves are not even in it — the block holds an ID, and the line went into the mod's strings file keyed by that ID.

The name you gave it is only for finding it again, and the mod's name is put in front of it. What the game follows is the GUID in each window's title.

steps.title: It is a v-mail until you say otherwise
steps.description:
Find treeType near the bottom of the tree window and change it to conversation.

A new tree comes out as a vmail — the template's default, and the wrong thing for two people talking. This is the single most common reason a new tree never appears in game.

steps.title: When the game goes looking for it
steps.description:
Set triggerPoint to whileTickOnTrackTarget.

That is the base game's answer for idle chatter: it is considered while the citizens are being simulated near you, rather than at some one-off moment like a v-mail arriving.

steps.title: And how often
steps.description:
Set treeChance to 0.25.

It arrives at 1, which means every eligible pair, every time — a city where nobody talks about anything else. A quarter is roughly what the base game's small talk uses.

Leave repeat at sixHours and priority at 3: the same pair will not have this conversation twice in an afternoon, and it will lose to anything the game considers more important.

steps.title: Who starts it
steps.description:
Expand participantA and set its connection to friend.

Participants are the roles, not the people — the game casts them when it looks for somewhere to play this. A is whoever speaks first.

steps.title: Where they have to be
steps.description:
Click the + beside A's triggers five times, and pick each entry from the dropdown it comes with: awake, noReactionState, indoors, publicLocation and sat.

A new entry arrives as the first name in the list, which is awake — so one of the five is already done.

All of them have to hold at once, so this comes to: awake, not reacting to anything, sitting down, indoors, somewhere public. Two people in a bar.

steps.title: And who they are talking to
steps.description:
Set participantB's connection to anyAcquaintance.

Looser than A on purpose. A has to be a friend of the person the game is building this around; B only has to be someone they know.

steps.title: B has less to satisfy
steps.description:
Give B three triggers the same way: awake, noReactionState and sat.

No indoors or publicLocation — A's conditions already settle where this is happening, and every condition you add to a participant is another reason for the game not to find a pair.

Leave C and D alone. They are not required, and this conversation has two people in it.

steps.title: The second thing said
steps.description:
Find messages and click the + beside it. A new message — and the block inside it — is written into the mod, and the entry points at it.

Nothing is asked, because nothing has to be. To use a message another tree already has instead, put its GUID in msgID afterwards.

steps.title: B answers
steps.description:
On the new entry messages.1, set saidBy to 1, saidTo to 0, and order to 1.

Those numbers are the participants: 0 is A, 1 is B. A new message arrives as A talking to B, so this one has to be turned around.

steps.title: What B says
steps.description:
Click the ➥ beside messages.1's msgID. The message opens in the middle window and its block opens on the right.

In that block, put Every night on my cruncher. into _ENG Localisation_ and click out of the box.

That row is not part of the file. It is the line looked up from the strings CSV, shown here so you can edit it in place — typing in it writes the CSV, not the block.

steps.title: A comes back
steps.description: Back on the tree window: + on messages again.

steps.title: A is already the speaker
steps.description:
On messages.2, set order to 2 and leave saidBy and saidTo as they are.

A new message is A talking to B, which is what this one is. Only the odd-numbered ones need turning around.

steps.title: What A asks
steps.description: Drill into messages.2 with ➥ and put Any good at it? in its block's _ENG Localisation_.

steps.title: B again
steps.description: + on messages again.

steps.title: Turned around again
steps.description: On messages.3: saidBy 1, saidTo 0, order 3.

steps.title: How good B claims to be
steps.description:
Drill into messages.3 and put I hold my own. in its block.

Deliberately flat. In a moment you will make this same line read three different ways depending on who is saying it.

steps.title: The last one
steps.description: + on messages one more time.

steps.title: A has the last word
steps.description: On messages.4, set order to 4. saidBy and saidTo are already right.

steps.title: How it ends
steps.description:
Drill into messages.4 and put Ain't no talking you into it? in its block.

Five messages exist now, and not one of them leads to another. Nothing about the order you made them in tells the game what follows what — that is next.

advanceWhen.contains: Ain't no talking you into it?

steps.title: Chain the first two
steps.description:
On messages.0, click the + beside links. Open the link it adds and set its to to messages.1.

That list is the messages in this tree, and what it writes is an instanceID. A message has two IDs: msgID names the document, and instanceID names this use of it in this tree. Links run between instances, so the same message can appear twice in a tree and be followed by something different each time — which is also why instanceID is the one field here you cannot type into.

steps.title: And the rest of the chain
steps.description:
Three more, the same way: messages.1 links to messages.2, 2 to 3, and 3 to 4.

from fills itself in — the editor knows which message you added the link to. Leave messages.4 with no links: that is what ends a conversation.

Check startingMessage at the bottom of the tree while you are here. It is the same list, and it already names messages.0 — which is how the game knows where to begin.

steps.title: Back to what B said first
steps.description:
Drill into messages.1 and then into its block, so Every night on my cruncher. is the line in the right-hand window.

A flat line for a flat citizen. Rather than write a second message for the keen ones, you hang alternatives off this block.

steps.title: The same line, from someone keen
steps.description:
Click the + beside replacements, and put Every night! I'm on a streak. in the _ENG Localisation_ row inside the new entry.

A replacement carries a line of its own, keyed by the replaceWithID beside it. That row writes the strings CSV exactly as the block's own line does.

advanceWhen.contains: Every night! I'm on a streak.

steps.title: Say who gets it
steps.description:
On replacements.0, set useTraits to true and add two traits: Char-Enthusiastic and Char-Cheerful. Leave traitCondition at IfAnyOfThese — either one will do.

Each row is the game's list of traits, searched by typing in it. What goes in the file is the bare name — not the REF:CharacterTrait|… form the case editor wants — and a trait your own mod defines is in the list too, above the game's.

steps.title: And from someone who has had enough
steps.description: A second replacement, the same way: line I quit. Rigged deck.

steps.title: For the sour ones
steps.description:
On replacements.1: useTraits true, traits Char-Pessimistic and Char-Spiteful.

One authored line now covers three kinds of person, and a citizen who is none of them gets the plain one. That is what makes the base game's chatter feel written rather than randomised.

steps.title: Do it again for the boast
steps.description: Drill into messages.3's block — I hold my own. — and add two replacements the same way, with the lines I'm unbeatable. and I lose every hand.

steps.title: And who they belong to
steps.description:
Set useTraits on both, and give them their traits: Char-Enthusiastic and Char-Cheerful for the boast, Char-Abrasive and Char-Pessimistic for the surrender.

Do not leave useTraits off. A replacement with no condition on it replaces the line for everybody, which is a roundabout way of rewriting the block.

steps.title: Now the ending
steps.description:
Drill into messages.4 and its block, so Ain't no talking you into it? is in the right-hand window.

This is the closing line, and it only really works if B has been sour. Next you give A something else to say — not a replacement this time, but a second block.

advanceWhen.is: Ain't no talking you into it?

steps.title: A second thing A might say
steps.description: On the message window in the middle, click the + beside blocks — a new block is written for you, as a new message was. Drill into it with ➥ and give it the line Deal me in next time.

steps.title: Let the game pick one
steps.description:
On the message window, set both blocks' alwaysDisplay to false and both their group to 1.

Blocks in a message normally all play, one after another — that is how a long document is built out of parts. Give two of them the same non-zero group and turn alwaysDisplay off, and the game picks one of the group instead.

steps.title: And spare the cheerful ones
steps.description:
Last thing, on the tree window. Open messages.3's links.0 — the link into the final message — and set useTraits to true, traits to Char-Cheerful and Char-Enthusiastic, and traitConditions to IfNoneOfThese.

Now the conversation only reaches its closing line when B is not one of those. A cheerful B answers the question and the chat simply stops there.

The gate is on the link, not on the message. That is the difference worth remembering: a trait on a block changes what is said, a trait on a link changes what happens next.

steps.title: That is a conversation
steps.description:
One tree, five messages, six blocks and ten lines of text — all of it in the panel on the left, and all of it in the mod.

Two citizens who know each other, sitting somewhere public, will now sometimes talk about Wizcards, and the conversation reads differently depending on which of them the game cast.

Worth trying from here: give participantA a jobs entry and set useJobs, so only certain workers have the conversation — that row is the same kind of list as traits, of the game's occupations; or open the tree's document and give it a background, a colour and a font — the same fields turn a tree into something the player reads rather than overhears.
